t: Maximum Number of Visible Points: Polar Angles, Wraparound, Two Pointers
o:
## Understanding the problem

Standing at location, you see a point iff its polar angle around you lies within an inclusive arc of width angle degrees; you may center that arc anywhere you like. Points sharing your exact coordinates are always visible regardless of rotation. Maximize how many points are visible.

Reduce every point to its angle atan2(dy, dx) measured from due east in degrees, normalized to [0, 360). Choosing the view arc becomes a one-dimensional circular problem: find the densest window of width angle over these angles.

**Example 1:** [[2,1],[2,2],[3,3]] around [1,1] sit at roughly 26.6, 45, and 45 degrees; a 90-degree arc centered near 45 catches all three.

**Example 2:** point [1,1] coincides with your position - always visible - and everything else fits one 90-degree window: answer 4.

**Example 3:** angles 180 and 45 differ by 135 degrees either way, exceeding angle = 13, so only one point can ever be seen.

Coordinates are small (<= 100) but n reaches 100000: computing n angles is trivial, yet an O(n^2) pairwise check is borderline - sorting the angles and sweeping is the safe route.
k: Visibility depends only on direction from your position, so collapse each point to atan2(dy, dx) degrees and ignore distances entirely.
Angles live on a circle; a window may straddle 0/360 degrees, handled by duplicating the sorted array shifted +360.
Points at your own location bypass geometry - count them separately and add at the end.

a.n: Approach 1: Fix One Edge, Count Inside (Brute Force)
a.i: Any maximal viewing arc can be rotated until its clockwise edge passes through some point. So for each point's angle a, count points j whose clockwise difference (a_j - a) mod 360 is at most angle; the best count over all anchors, plus co-located points, is the answer. This directly translates the definition and doubles as the correctness reference.
s: Compute every angle relative to location via atan2; tally co-located points separately.
For each anchor angle a, scan all other angles.
Clockwise difference d = ((a_j - a) mod 360 + 360) mod 360; increment when d <= angle.
Track the maximum count; return max + coLocated.
a.t: O(n^2) - for each anchor direction, a full scan of all points.

a.i: Sort the angles and append a +360 copy of each, unwrapping the circle into a line. The densest arc becomes the densest window [a_i, a_i + angle], found with two pointers advancing monotonically. Floating-point comparisons get a tiny epsilon; co-located points simply add on top.
s: Collect angles of all points not at location; sort them.
Duplicate the array appending a +360 copy of every element.
For each right pointer, advance left while angles[right] - angles[left] > angle + eps.
Best window size = max(right - left + 1) over the sweep.
Return best + number of co-located points.
a.t: O(n log n) - sorting dominates; the two-pointer sweep is linear.

w:
Jump to Approach 2 quickly; Approach 1 mainly serves as the correctness reference. Narrate the unwrap-the-circle trick - interviewers appreciate why doubling the sorted angles removes wraparound cases.

**Pitfalls.** Floating-point fuzz at window edges - compare against angle + 1e-9; forgetting co-located points when ALL points coincide (the angle list is empty); mishandling angle = 0 (only equal angles fit, which the two-pointer logic already covers); mixing radians and degrees.

**Follow-ups.** Stream points through a sliding window over a circular buffer of angles; report the actual viewing direction achieving the maximum; extend to obstacles blocking sightlines.
